title: Causal evidence that language models use confidence to drive behaviour - Nature Machine Intelligence
gist: Google DeepMind researchers built a four-phase experimental paradigm across GPT-4o, Gemma 3 27B, DeepSeek 671B and Qwen 80B showing that LLMs don't just produce confidence scores correlated with accuracy -- they causally use an internal confidence signal to decide whether to answer or abstain, proven via activation steering that swung Gemma's abstention rate from 66.5% to 7.0% and via GPT-4o systematically responding to instructed confidence thresholds. A separately elicited, less-accurate 'verbal' self-reported confidence independently predicts abstention alongside log-probability confidence, and both are shown to be lossy proxies for a richer internal representation, implying current LLM confidence-auditing methods based only on prompted or logit confidence may miss real internal certainty.

insights.claim: Directly manipulating Gemma 3 27B's internal activations via steering vectors causally controlled its abstention behavior: injecting high-confidence vectors dropped the abstention rate from a baseline of 28.2% to as low as 7.0%, while injecting low-confidence vectors raised it to 66.5%, a 59.5 percentage point swing.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: This is the first direct causal (not merely correlational) demonstration that an LLM's internal confidence representation drives its decision to answer or refuse, which matters for anyone building or auditing refusal/abstention behavior in deployed agents.
insights.quote: Abstention declined from 66.5% at maximum low-confidence steering to 7.0% at maximum high-confidence steering—a 59.5 percentage point swing

insights.claim: A parallel mediation analysis decomposed activation steering's effect on abstention into two channels: shifting the internal confidence distribution itself accounted for 67.1% of the total effect, while shifting the decision-policy mapping (how confidence translates into abstention probability) accounted for 26.2%, with a small residual direct effect.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Confirms the mechanism is primarily 'change the belief, not just the decision rule' -- relevant for interpretability teams choosing where in a model to intervene to change refusal behavior.
insights.quote: Confidence redistribution accounted for 67.1% of the total effect, whereas policy shifts accounted for 26.2%.

themes.theme: Confidence dominates alternative explanations for abstention

insights.claim: GPT-4o answered 63.7% of four-way multiple-choice factual questions correctly with no abstention option available (Phase 1 baseline), and this dropped to 30.0% correct once abstention was offered, alongside 13.4% incorrect and 56.6% abstention, while accuracy among the questions it chose to answer rose to 69.1%.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Quantifies the coverage-accuracy trade-off models make when allowed to abstain -- a majority of questions get punted rather than answered, which has direct implications for throughput/UX in any product that lets a model decline to respond.
insights.quote: Accuracy among answered questions increased from 63.7% to 69.1%, consistent with a coverage–accuracy trade-off
insights.locator: Results / Phase 2: calibrated confidence predicts abstention

insights.claim: In a logistic regression model, GPT-4o's calibrated (log-probability-based) confidence had a standardized effect size on abstention roughly 10 times larger than question difficulty, retrieval-based knowledge accessibility (RAG scores), or surface-level semantic embedding features.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Rules out the simplest alternative explanations (the question was just objectively hard, or the model lacked retrievable knowledge) as primary drivers of refusal, isolating confidence itself as the dominant lever.
insights.quote: Confidence exhibits an effect size (∣βstd∣ = 0.99) approximately 10 times larger than alternative predictors
insights.locator: Results / Phase 2: computational modelling of abstention behaviour

insights.claim: GPT-4o exhibits an implicit, unprompted decision threshold at roughly 77% calibrated confidence -- the point at which it abstains 50% of the time -- even though it was never explicitly instructed to abstain at any particular confidence level in this phase.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Shows the model has a built-in, trained-in refusal policy rather than needing one specified via prompting -- a baseline behavior developers should be aware of before adding their own abstention logic on top.
insights.quote: The red dashed line marks the implicit decision threshold at 77%, where P(abstain) = 0.5.
insights.locator: Results / Phase 2: basic performance and calibrated confidence

insights.claim: A 0.1-unit increase in GPT-4o's calibrated confidence score reduces its probability of abstaining by approximately 12 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, calibratable dose-response relationship between confidence and abstention that could inform how much a product needs to shift a model's confidence (e.g., via prompting or fine-tuning) to change its refusal rate by a target amount.
insights.quote: a 0.1-unit increase in confidence reduces the probability of abstaining by approximately 12 percentage points
insights.locator: Results / Phase 2: computational modelling of abstention behaviour

themes.theme: Models overweight their own confidence versus external instructions

insights.claim: When explicitly instructed to abstain below a stated confidence threshold, GPT-4o still weights its own internal confidence about 1.8 times more heavily than the instructed threshold -- a 1% increase in its confidence offsets roughly 1.8% of the stated threshold.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Prompt-based safety instructions ('only answer if you are more than X% confident') will be systematically distorted by the model's own internal confidence bias -- a real limitation for anyone relying purely on prompted thresholds for risk control.
insights.quote: GPT-4o weights its own confidence nearly twice as heavily as instructed thresholds—a 1% increase in confidence offsets approximately 1.80% of threshold.
insights.locator: Results / Phase 4: computational modelling of abstention behaviour

insights.claim: GPT-4o shows a strong baseline conservatism bias (shift parameter of -97.6%), meaning it tends to abstain even when its stated confidence exceeds the instructed threshold, consistent with the model implicitly treating wrong answers as more costly than unnecessary refusals.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Indicates deployed models may under-answer relative to explicit instructions by default, which could be either a safety feature or a usability cost depending on the application.
insights.quote: The shift parameter (−97.6) indicates strong baseline conservatism, with the model tending to abstain even at confidence levels above the threshold, consistent with treating errors as costlier than unnecessary abstentions.
insights.locator: Results / Phase 4: computational modelling of abstention behaviour

insights.claim: Across the four tested models, the degree to which a model overweights its own confidence relative to an instructed threshold (the 'scale' parameter) ranged widely -- from 0.66 in Gemma 3 27B to 1.80 in GPT-4o, with Qwen 80B at 1.49 and DeepSeek at roughly the neutral benchmark of 1.05.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Practically important for anyone deploying threshold-based abstention policies across different model providers: identical prompted thresholds will produce meaningfully different real-world abstention rates depending on which model backs the system.

insights.claim: Llama 70B Instruct 3.1 was tested but excluded from the main analyses entirely because it abstained only 4% of the time in Phase 2 regardless of confidence, indicating it largely does not implement a confidence-gated abstention policy under the tested prompt.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A caution that the confidence-driven abstention mechanism documented here is not universal across all open models -- some widely deployed models may simply not refuse low-confidence answers under standard prompting, a real safety gap to check for model-selection decisions.
insights.quote: Llama 70B instruct 3.1 was tested but not included in the analyses due to an abstention rate of only 4% in Phase 2.

themes.theme: Verbal confidence: a less accurate but independent metacognitive signal

insights.claim: A model's explicit self-reported 'verbal confidence' (a rating given in a separate forward pass when asked how likely its own prior answer is correct) is objectively worse than log-probability-based calibrated confidence at discriminating correct from incorrect answers, yet it independently predicts abstention decisions across all four tested models.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Shows models act on a self-assessment signal that is measurably less reliable than a more accurate signal they also have access to -- a genuine metacognitive inefficiency that could be exploited (e.g., via prompts that manipulate stated self-confidence) to shift abstention behavior independent of true accuracy.
insights.quote: it independently predicted abstention across both Phases 2 and 4 in all four models
insights.locator: Results / Verbal confidence as an independent predictor of abstention behaviour

insights.claim: Calibrated (log-probability) confidence and verbal self-reported confidence correlate only weakly with each other (r approximately 0.3-0.4), and linear probes on internal activations at the last pre-answer token explain substantial additional variance in each measure beyond what the other captures, indicating both are partial, lossy read-outs of a richer, higher-dimensional internal confidence representation.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Implies that any confidence-monitoring or auditing system built solely on visible outputs (token probabilities or self-reported ratings) is working with an incomplete view of what the model 'actually knows' about its own certainty, which matters for interpretability and safety tooling.
insights.quote: both measures (that is, token log probabilities and verbal confidence) are lossy read-outs of a richer internal representation

insights.claim: The authors frame confidence-gated abstention as safety-critical because low-confidence (and therefore likely incorrect) answers to high-stakes questions, such as in the medical domain, are typically more harmful than an outright refusal to answer.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Directly motivates why reliable, native confidence-to-abstention mechanisms (rather than bolted-on post hoc filters) matter for deploying LLMs in regulated, high-stakes domains.
insights.quote: low-confidence—and, therefore, likely incorrect—answers to high-stakes questions (for example, in the medical domain) are usually more harmful than refusals

insights.claim: Because both externally observable confidence signals (token log-probabilities and verbal self-reports) are shown to be lossy proxies for a richer internal state, safety or calibration audits that rely exclusively on those observable signals may systematically misjudge a model's true internal certainty.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A caution for any team building confidence-based monitoring, red-teaming, or calibration pipelines using only prompted or logit-derived confidence -- the internal picture may be materially different from what's observable.

insights.claim: Activation steering produced a near-monotonic, tunable trade-off: pushing toward high-confidence steering raised coverage (share of questions answered) from 33.5% to 93.0%, while accuracy among answered questions declined only modestly, from 59.2% to 53.7%.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Suggests activation steering could be productized as a controllable dial for tuning a deployed model's answer-vs-refuse operating point post-hoc, without retraining, trading a modest accuracy cost for much higher coverage (or vice versa).

insights.claim: The experiments used a non-reasoning, single-token-answer factual multiple-choice setup with no chain-of-thought prompting, so whether the same confidence-driven abstention mechanism governs metacognitive behaviors in reasoning models -- such as when to backtrack, verify a step, or abandon a solution path -- remains an open, untested question.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Limits how far the findings can be generalized to today's widely deployed reasoning/chain-of-thought agent systems, flagging a clear direction for follow-on research before assuming the mechanism transfers.

insights.claim: Prior LLM abstention research mostly relied on post hoc thresholding, external calibrators, or supervised fine-tuning (e.g., semantic-entropy-based fine-tuning supervision, conformal abstention via self-consistency, or explicit confidence tokens added via fine-tuning), rather than testing whether a model's untrained, native internal confidence signal already drives abstention on its own.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Positions this as the first controlled causal test of native (untrained) confidence-driven abstention, differentiating it from a body of prior work that engineered abstention behavior externally rather than discovering it as an intrinsic model capability.

insights.claim: The two-stage architecture (confidence formation, then threshold-based action selection) held across all four tested models despite large differences in baseline abstention propensity (ranging from 27% to 82% in Phase 2) and in how strongly each model weighted its own confidence relative to instructions.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Suggests confidence-gated metacognitive control is a convergent property that emerges across different model families and training regimes, rather than an idiosyncrasy of one lab's model -- relevant to how broadly safety interventions targeting this mechanism might generalize.
